scenes.tts: How can a single gray-green patch on a tree show different kinds of symbiosis? Start with the patch, then look closely inside it.
scenes.visual: Hook first. A large GREY tree trunk fills the frame while one pale lichen patch slowly spreads. The camera pushes toward the patch. A question mark grows from the patch. COLOUR MAP FOR BOTH FILMS: fungus BLUE; alga or cyanobacterium GREEN; trees and plants GOLD; sugar and plant food YELLOW; minerals TEAL; harm RED; unaffected GREY; water pale BLUE. Help is shown by a white plus badge, not a colour. All biological drawings are labelled cartoons, and any outcome meter is labelled 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: How can a single gray-green patch on a tree show different kinds of symbiosis? Start with the patch, then look closely inside it.

scenes.visual: Title card 'One Patch, Two Relationships' appears over the same moving trunk. The lichen continues a slow outward ripple behind the title.

scenes.tts: This patch is a lichen. Its main partners are a fungus and an alga, or sometimes a cyanobacterium. They remain different species while sharing a common body. That long-lasting, close relationship is symbiosis.
scenes.visual: The patch opens like a hinged cutaway. BLUE fungus threads form most of the body around GREEN round cells. Labels 'fungus' and 'alga or cyanobacterium' settle beside them. Separate species badges stay attached while a bracket labelled 'one lichen body' surrounds both. The trunk drifts slowly behind the cutaway.
scenes.narration: This patch is a lichen. Its main partners are a fungus and an alga, or sometimes a cyanobacterium. They remain different species while sharing a common body. That long-lasting, close relationship is symbiosis.

scenes.tts: Watch what moves. The photosynthetic partner makes sugar, which feeds both partners. Fungus threads shelter those cells and help keep them moist. Rainwater spreads through the lichen body. Each partner gains something.
scenes.visual: GREEN cells brighten under a simple sun icon. YELLOW sugar dots move from the cells into BLUE fungus threads. Pale BLUE water droplets land, spread through the cutaway, and remain around the GREEN cells. White plus badges rise beside both partner labels while a small outcome strip reads 'both helped'.
scenes.narration: Watch what moves. The photosynthetic partner makes sugar, which feeds both partners. Fungus threads shelter those cells and help keep them moist. Rainwater spreads through the lichen body. Each partner gains something.

scenes.tts: Close contact matters. A bird may eat a seed and fly away. That brief meeting is not symbiosis with the plant. Lichen partners remain together, often for a long time.
scenes.visual: The lichen holds at left. At right, a simple bird takes one seed and flies off along a short dashed path. A label 'brief meeting' follows the bird and gets a soft cross. The lichen gains a long looping time arrow labelled 'close contact'.
scenes.narration: Close contact matters. A bird may eat a seed and fly away. That brief meeting is not symbiosis with the plant. Lichen partners remain together, often for a long time.

scenes.tts: When all partners benefit, the relationship is mutualism. Now zoom back out. The whole lichen sits on tree bark. The lichen gains a place to live. What does the tree gain or lose?
scenes.visual: The cutaway closes into the original patch. A label 'mutualism inside the lichen' follows it during the zoom outward. The whole lichen gains a white plus badge. Beside the GOLD tree, a three-position outcome meter labelled 'helped / unaffected / harmed — schematic' waits with no selection.
scenes.narration: When all partners benefit, the relationship is mutualism. Now zoom back out. The whole lichen sits on tree bark. The lichen gains a place to live. What does the tree gain or lose?

scenes.visual: Hold the lichen's plus badge and the tree's unselected schematic meter. A ring fills slowly around the question mark. The trunk texture continues moving gently.

scenes.tts: For ordinary lichens on bark, the tree seems unaffected. Experts say these lichens almost never harm the tree. When a partner benefits and the other is unaffected, the relationship is commensalism.
scenes.visual: The GOLD tree's outcome meter slides to GREY 'seems unaffected'. The word 'seems' pulses once. A bracket joins the lichen plus badge and tree grey dash, transforming into the label 'commensalism: lichen and tree'. The inside label remains faintly visible within the patch.
scenes.narration: For ordinary lichens on bark, the tree seems unaffected. Experts say these lichens almost never harm the tree. When a partner benefits and the other is unaffected, the relationship is commensalism.

scenes.tts: Sort symbiosis by what each partner gains or loses. That rule separates the relationships hiding in the same patch. It also handles harmful partnerships, as long as the partners live together closely.
scenes.visual: The lichen picture shifts left but stays large. On the right, an outcome board grows from the same badges: 'both helped' becomes 'mutualism'; 'helped plus unaffected' becomes 'commensalism'; 'helped plus harmed' remains blank. The rule writes across the top, then the blank row glows RED at one end.
scenes.narration: Sort symbiosis by what each partner gains or loses. That rule separates the relationships hiding in the same patch. It also handles harmful partnerships, as long as the partners live together closely.

scenes.tts: A blacklegged tick can stay on a deer and drink blood for days. The tick gains food. The deer loses blood and may get irritated skin. This helped-harmed pattern is parasitism.
scenes.visual: The outcome board transforms into a labelled cartoon deer skin filling the lower frame. A small dark BROWN tick (outside the colour map, so it is never read as fungus) grips the skin while RED blood drops move toward it. A white plus badge rises beside 'tick'; a RED harm badge settles beside 'deer'. The blank row fills with 'parasitism'.
scenes.narration: A blacklegged tick can stay on a deer and drink blood for days. The tick gains food. The deer loses blood and may get irritated skin. This helped-harmed pattern is parasitism.

scenes.tts: A parasite is not the same as a predator. A predator usually kills prey during a brief attack. A parasite usually feeds for days or longer without killing its host.
scenes.visual: Keep the tick-deer pair on the left under a long time bar. On the right, a schematic hawk crosses quickly toward a mouse under a short time bar. Labels transform from 'long close feeding' and 'brief attack' into 'parasite' and 'predator'.
scenes.narration: A parasite is not the same as a predator. A predator usually kills prey during a brief attack. A parasite usually feeds for days or longer without killing its host.

scenes.tts: None of these partners chooses kindness or harm. Ways of living can continue when they support survival and reproduction. Mutualism can support both partners. Parasitism can support the parasite while harming its host.
scenes.visual: A thought bubble reading 'kind?' appears over the fungus, then folds away. The lichen and tick-deer cartoons move along separate looping arrows labelled 'survive' and 'reproduce'. White plus badges travel with both lichen partners; only the tick's plus badge continues on the parasite loop while the deer's RED badge remains.
scenes.narration: None of these partners chooses kindness or harm. Ways of living can continue when they support survival and reproduction. Mutualism can support both partners. Parasitism can support the parasite while harming its host.

scenes.tts: The names describe outcomes, not personalities. Mutualism is the helped-helped pattern. Commensalism is helped-unaffected. Parasitism is helped-harmed. Other outcome pairs do not match these taught kinds.
scenes.visual: The survival loops flatten into the outcome board. White plus-plus badges slide into 'mutualism'. White plus and GREY dash slide into 'commensalism'. White plus and RED harm badge slide into 'parasitism'. Faint remaining pairs move below a line labelled 'not these taught kinds'.
scenes.narration: The names describe outcomes, not personalities. Mutualism is the helped-helped pattern. Commensalism is helped-unaffected. Parasitism is helped-harmed. Other outcome pairs do not match these taught kinds.

scenes.tts: So begin with partners, not labels. Follow what each receives, what each gives, and whether either is harmed. Then the name follows from the outcomes you can support.
scenes.visual: Return to the trunk with the lichen cutaway nested inside the patch and the tick-deer example beside it. A white path moves through labelled stops: 'name partners', 'trace outcomes', 'choose kind'. The last stop becomes a question mark, ready for the lesson's simulation.
scenes.narration: So begin with partners, not labels. Follow what each receives, what each gives, and whether either is harmed. Then the name follows from the outcomes you can support.

scenes.visual: End card shows one line only: 'Sort symbiosis by what each partner gains or loses.' No subtitle, site name, title, or smaller line. The lichen patch continues a faint living ripple behind the text.
